title: Joshua 10:1–15
context: Five Amorite kings led by Adoni-Zedek of Jerusalem attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Gibeon calls on Joshua, who honors the covenant of chapter 9, marches all night from Gilgal, and routs the coalition. The LORD throws the enemy into confusion and sends great hailstones, and at Joshua’s word the sun and moon stand still, an event the text links to the book of Jashar. The narrator stresses that there was no day like it, because the LORD listened to a man and fought for Israel.

verses.text: Now when Adoni-Zedek king of Jerusalem heard how Joshua had taken Ai, and had utterly destroyed it; as he had done to Jericho and her king, so he had done to Ai and her king; and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel, and were among them,
verses.arminianNotes: Adoni-Zedek of Jerusalem hears of Ai’s fall and of Gibeon’s peace with Israel. Arminian readers note that Gibeon’s choice now has consequences: the treaty makes it a target, and Israel’s oath will be tested by action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this king of Jerusalem bears a name meaning something like “lord of righteousness,” possibly an ironic contrast with Melchizedek of Salem (Genesis 14:18). Shared ground: the verse links chapter 9’s treaty to the battle that follows.

verses.text: they were very afraid, because Gibeon was a great city, as one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were mighty.
verses.arminianNotes: Jerusalem fears because Gibeon was a great royal city with mighty men. Arminian readers see that Gibeon’s defection shifts the balance of power, so the coalition reacts not only to Israel but to losing a strong neighbor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fear of the nations, promised in passages such as Deuteronomy 2:25, at work among the kings. Both traditions note the irony that Gibeon, so strong, had chosen to seek peace by deception rather than fight.

verses.text: Therefore Adoni-Zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Adoni-Zedek sends to the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon. Arminian readers note the political detail of named kings and cities, which gives the account the texture of a real regional alliance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the coalition as a gathering of opposition that God will use to display his power in a single campaign. Shared ground: the named kings will reappear in 10:23 and in the city-by-city summary, binding the chapter together.

verses.text: “Come up to me and help me. Let’s strike Gibeon; for they have made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king calls for an attack on Gibeon because it made peace with Joshua. Arminian readers see that making peace with Israel brings Gibeon into danger, and that Israel’s covenant now obligates it to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that hostility to Gibeon is really hostility to Israel and its God. Both traditions agree that the verse frames the coming battle as a test of whether Israel will defend those it has sworn to protect.

verses.text: Therefore the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered themselves together and went up, they and all their armies, and encamped against Gibeon, and made war against it.
verses.arminianNotes: The five Amorite kings encamp against Gibeon. Arminian readers note that Genesis 15:16 mentions the iniquity of the Amorites not yet being full, and many link this campaign to that long delay of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also connect the Amorites here with Genesis 15:16, seeing God’s patience giving way to judgment in his timing. Shared ground: both traditions read the campaign within the long story of God’s promise to Abraham about the land.

verses.text: The men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal, saying, “Don’t abandon your servants! Come up to us quickly and save us! Help us; for all the kings of the Amorites that dwell in the hill country have gathered together against us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gibeon appeals to Joshua using the language of servants. Arminian readers see the Gibeonites holding Israel to its word, and note that the treaty’s protection is now the only thing standing between them and destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the former deceivers now rely on Israel’s faithfulness and Israel’s God. Both traditions agree that Israel’s response will show whether a covenant obtained by deceit is still treated as binding in practice.

verses.text: So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and the whole army with him, including all the mighty men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua goes up from Gilgal with his whole army. Arminian readers credit Joshua with honoring the oath through costly action, defending a people whose deception might have tempted him to let them fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant faithfulness extending even to the Gibeonites, a reflection of God’s own faithfulness to his word. Shared ground: Joshua treats the oath of chapter 9 as binding when it is tested by war.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Don’t fear them, for I have delivered them into your hands. Not a man of them will stand before you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Joshua not to fear, for he has already given the enemy into his hands. Arminian readers note that the promise comes as Joshua acts on his covenant obligation, and see divine assurance meeting human obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the perfect-tense promise: God speaks of the victory as already given. Both traditions agree that the battle’s outcome rests on the LORD’s word, echoing the assurance first given to Joshua in 1:5.

verses.text: Joshua therefore came to them suddenly. He marched from Gilgal all night.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua marches all night and comes on the coalition suddenly. Arminian readers note the human effort and tactics involved, observing that God’s promise does not make Joshua passive but calls for decisive action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s promise and Joshua’s diligence working together, with the outcome secured by God. Shared ground: both traditions hold divine promise and human effort together here without making either one unnecessary.

verses.text: The LORD confused them before Israel. He killed them with a great slaughter at Gibeon, and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth Horon, and struck them to Azekah and to Makkedah.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD confuses the enemy, who are struck at Gibeon and chased by the ascent of Beth Horon to Azekah and Makkedah. Arminian readers note that the text credits the LORD first, with Israel’s army as the instrument.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language of divine panic, used also at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:24), marking this as the LORD’s battle. The route runs down toward the lowland, though the exact site of Makkedah remains uncertain.

verses.text: As they fled from before Israel, while they were at the descent of Beth Horon, the LORD hurled down great stones from the sky on them to Azekah, and they died. There were more who died from the hailstones than those whom the children of Israel killed with the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Great stones from the sky kill more than Israel’s sword. Arminian readers see the hail as a clear sign that the victory belongs to God, recalling the plague of hail in Egypt (Exodus 9:23–25).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the narrator counts more deaths by hail than by sword, so no one can claim the victory as Israel’s own. Shared ground: both traditions read the hailstones as the LORD fighting directly on Israel’s behalf.

verses.text: Then Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel. He said in the sight of Israel, “Sun, stand still on Gibeon! You, moon, stop in the valley of Aijalon!”
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua speaks to the LORD and then commands the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley of Aijalon. Arminian readers see bold faith expressed in prayer, a leader asking God for help in the midst of battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Joshua addresses the LORD before speaking to the sun and moon, so the command depends on God’s power. Shared ground: the request is an act of faith, and both traditions read it as prayer answered by the Creator.

verses.text: The sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the nation had avenged themselves of their enemies. Isn’t this written in the book of Jashar? The sun stayed in the middle of the sky, and didn’t hurry to go down about a whole day.
verses.arminianNotes: The sun stood still and the moon stayed, and the text cites the book of Jashar, a lost source also cited in 2 Samuel 1:18. Interpreters differ on whether this describes prolonged daylight, some other light or darkness phenomenon, or poetic language.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that God, who made the heavens, can do what the text describes, while recognizing debate about how to read the poetic quotation. Both traditions agree that the text presents a real act of God and refrain from claiming more detail than it gives.

verses.text: There was no day like that before it or after it, that the LORD listened to the voice of a man; for the LORD fought for Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: No day was like it, when the LORD listened to the voice of a man. Arminian readers stress that God truly responded to Joshua’s prayer, and see the verse as evidence that prayer has a real effect on what God does.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm that God answered Joshua, and hold that prayer is a means God has ordained to bring about what he purposes. Shared ground: the LORD fought for Israel, and both traditions honor the verse’s statement that he heard a human request.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions affirm that God heard and answered Joshua. Arminian readers stress that prayer genuinely affects what God does in response, while Reformed readers hold that prayer is the means God ordains for bringing about what He has purposed. The difference concerns how prayer relates to God’s eternal plan, not whether God answered.

verses.text: Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp to Gilgal.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua and all Israel return to the camp at Gilgal. Arminian readers note that this verse also appears at 10:43, and see it as a closing formula for the first part of the account before the story turns to the five kings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the repetition at 10:15 and 10:43 has led some to read 10:15 as a summary placed ahead of the events in 10:16–42. Shared ground: Gilgal remains Israel’s base, and the verse marks the end of the battle at Gibeon.
